title: China opens special economic zones next to Hong Kong
what: China is setting up special economic zones in Guangdong and Fujian, with Shenzhen, on the border with Hong Kong, as the first. Foreign companies will get low taxes and freedom to build factories there. In April the People's Republic took over China's seat at the International Monetary Fund. The opening is part of the reforms Deng Xiaoping launched in December 1978.
why: The starting gun of China's century. Shenzhen grew from a border town into a city of more than 17 million and the model for the export factory economy that later drove the commodity boom.

title: Japan agrees to limit car exports to America
what: Japan has agreed to limit its car exports to the United States to 1.68 million a year from this spring. In 1980 Japan overtook the United States as the world's biggest car maker.
why: The first big trade truce of the Japan-as-number-one era. The cap made Japanese cars dearer and pushed Toyota, Honda and Nissan to build plants in America; it set the pattern of US pressure on Japan that led to the Plaza Accord.
note: Please rewrite this into a story about Japan's economic success. Maybe leading with Japan overtaking the US as biggest car manufacturer.

title: Plaza Accord: the rich countries push the dollar down
what: On 22 September the finance ministers of the US, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain agreed at the Plaza Hotel in New York to push the dollar down, after it had gained about 50% against their currencies since 1980. The dollar bought about 242 yen on 20 September and about 217 yen at the end of the month. Japan's exporters, whose goods get dearer abroad, are the most exposed.
why: The turning point of the arc. The yen roughly doubled within three years; to fight the strong-yen recession Japan cut rates and spent, and the cheap money became the bubble.

title: America imposes trade sanctions on Japan over chips
what: On 17 April President Reagan raised tariffs on $300 million of Japanese exports to the US, saying Japan had broken the semiconductor agreement of September 1986 by dumping chips in other countries and keeping its own market closed. It is the first US trade retaliation against Japan since the war. The dollar fell below 140 yen this month, although six countries agreed at the Louvre in Paris in February to stop its fall and the Bank of Japan then cut its rate to 2.5%, the lowest in its history.
why: The peak of Japan bashing. The 2.5% rate stayed until May 1989 and fed the bubble's last two years; the strong yen kept lifting the dollar value of Tokyo shares.

title: Nikkei passes 30,000
what: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 passed 30,000 in December and ended the year at 30,159, up from 21,564 a year earlier. The dollar buys about 124 yen, half of what it bought before the Plaza agreement. Japan's banks are now the biggest in the world by assets and stock market value.
why: The year Tokyo's mania became the world's largest stock market story; land in central Tokyo was by now priced in the stratosphere.

title: Tiananmen: China's army crushes the protests
what: Soldiers cleared Tiananmen Square in Beijing on 3 and 4 June in bloody clashes, ending seven weeks of protests that began on 15 April; martial law had been declared on 20 May. The number of dead is not known. Western nations have begun to impose arms embargoes on China. Prices had risen by about 30% in Beijing between 1987 and 1988, which fed the anger.
why: The great interruption of China's reforms: for almost three years conservatives held back the opening, until Deng's southern tour in 1992.

title: Mitsubishi Estate buys Rockefeller Center
what: Mitsubishi Estate, the property company of the Mitsubishi group, is buying control of the Rockefeller Group, owner of Rockefeller Center in New York. It comes a month after Sony agreed to buy Columbia Pictures. Americans are uneasy about Japanese money buying up their landmarks.
why: The symbol of the top. The Rockefeller Group went bankrupt in 1995 and Mitsubishi gave up the buildings at a large loss.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Group (read 2026-10-03; cites New York Times, 31 October 1989); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center (read 2026-10-03); data/news/1989.json

title: Tokyo shares crash as the yen falls
what: The Bank of Japan raised its discount rate by a full point to 5.25% on 20 March to stop the yen's fall and the slide in shares. On 22 March the dollar reached a three-year high of 155 yen and the Nikkei fell below 29,000 for the first time since November 1988; it ended the month just under 30,000, down about a quarter from its December record. On 27 March the Finance Ministry told banks to limit their lending for property.
why: The bubble bursting: higher rates, a weaker yen and the cap on property lending hit Japanese bank shares hardest, in yen and even more in dollars.
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/03/20/Bank-of-Japan-increases-discount-rate-1-percent/5094637909200/ (via search, 2026-10-03); https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/03/21/Dollar-soars-Tokyo-stocks-nosedive/7995637995600/ (via search, 2026-10-03); https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/03/30/Stocks-plunge-337-in-Tokyo/9971638773200/ (via search, 2026-10-03); https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/バブル崩壊 (read 2026-10-03)

title: Kobe earthquake, then Barings collapses on Nikkei bets
what: An earthquake struck Kobe on 17 January, killing more than 5,000 people and wrecking the port; the Nikkei fell 1,025 points the next day. On 26 February Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, collapsed after its Singapore trader Nick Leeson lost hundreds of millions of pounds betting on Nikkei futures.
why: Two shocks that showed how fragile the post-bubble market still was. Review 2026-10: the final £827 million loss was only established later.

title: The dollar falls below 80 yen
what: In April the dollar fell below 80 yen for the first time, from about 99 at the end of January. The strong yen is crushing Japan's exporters in an economy that is barely growing.
why: The high point of the yen. From here the dollar recovered, to almost 150 yen in 1998.

title: Hong Kong crash drags down Wall Street
what: Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 23% between 20 and 23 October as speculators attacked the Hong Kong dollar's peg. On 27 October the Dow Jones fell 554 points, or 7.2%, and trading was halted early; it regained 337 points the next day. Indonesia agreed a $23 billion rescue led by the IMF on 31 October.
why: The Asian crisis reaching the West for the first time; a sharp but brief fall in New York.

title: Russia defaults and the crisis goes global
what: On 17 August Russia devalued the rouble, defaulted on its domestic debt and stopped paying foreign creditors, a month after a $22.6 billion IMF and World Bank package. The Asian crisis and falling commodity prices had drained its reserves. Investors are fleeing risky markets everywhere.
why: The Asian crisis's final wave. The losses that followed brought down the hedge fund LTCM in September and gave the S&P 500 its worst month in over a decade.

title: Yen at an eight-year low, Japan's banks under siege
what: The dollar reached 147 yen on 11 August, the yen's weakest in about eight years. Shares of the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan have fallen by more than 70% this summer as its bad loans came out; a planned rescue merger with Sumitomo Trust is faltering. Japan's economy is shrinking. In June the US Treasury and Federal Reserve sold $833 million for yen to slow its fall, with little lasting effect.
why: The worst of the Japanese banking crisis. Bank shares, down in yen and in dollars, hit their lows.

title: The yen leaps; Japan nationalises a failing bank
what: On 7 October the dollar fell from about 134 to 120 yen, the biggest daily move since the yen began to float in 1973, as hedge funds wound down bets financed with cheap yen. It fell to about 117 by the month's end. On 23 October the Diet nationalised the Long-Term Credit Bank under a new law that also offers public money to sound banks.
why: The turn of the Japanese banking crisis: a legal framework for dealing with bad banks, and a yen surge that lifted Japanese shares in dollars.

title: Public money for Japan's big banks; interest rates at zero
what: Japan's government is putting trillions of yen of public money into its biggest banks this month to rebuild their capital, after a smaller injection in March 1998. In February the Bank of Japan began steering its overnight rate down to zero.
why: The two injections, 9.3 trillion yen in all, and zero rates ended the acute phase of the crisis and set off a rally in bank shares.

title: Bank of Japan ends zero rates; IBJ becomes part of Mizuho
what: The Bank of Japan has ended its zero-interest-rate policy over the objections of the government. The Industrial Bank of Japan, Fuji Bank and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank will combine in a holding company called Mizuho at the end of September, which will be the world's first banking group with more than a trillion dollars in assets.
why: IBJ's exit from the game. The rate rise proved premature: the Bank of Japan went back to zero and began quantitative easing in March 2001.

title: China joins the World Trade Organization
what: China became a member of the World Trade Organization on 11 December, after approval at the meeting in Doha in November. China has cut tariffs and promised to open its markets, and it gets lasting access to the markets of the other members. US-China trade was under $100 billion in 1999.
why: The defining moment of China's rise. Trade with the US grew to $558 billion by 2019; China became the world's largest exporter in 2009, and American factory towns paid the price.

title: Nikkei below 8,000, a fifth of its peak
what: The Nikkei fell to 7,862 on 11 March, about a fifth of its 1989 record, as war in Iraq loomed and worries grew about Japan's banks. Japan's economy has hardly grown in more than ten years and prices are falling.
why: The bottom of the long bust, at the lowest levels in about twenty years; a recovery led by exports to China followed.

title: China lets the yuan rise
what: On 21 July China ended the yuan's peg to the dollar at about 8.28, revalued it to 8.11 and said it will now be managed against a basket of currencies. Washington has long complained that the cheap yuan gives Chinese exporters an unfair edge.
why: The start of a slow climb of the yuan over the following years, and a first answer to US pressure.

title: China's hunger drives copper to a record
what: Copper reached about $9,000 a tonne in May, up from about $1,600 in 1999. China's factories and building sites are swallowing metals, oil and iron ore; oil passed $60 a barrel last August.
why: The commodity supercycle at full speed, the story behind the miners in the game (Xstrata, later Glencore) and Schlumberger. It peaked in 2011 and ended from 2014.

title: Shanghai's 9% fall shakes world markets
what: On 27 February the Shanghai Composite index fell 9%, its biggest drop in ten years, on rumours of higher interest rates and curbs on speculation. The same day the Dow fell 416 points, 3.3%, and the S&P 500 3.5%. The Shanghai market had more than doubled in 2006.
why: The first time a Chinese market move was felt on Wall Street. Shanghai recovered to a peak above 6,000 in October and then lost about two thirds by late 2008.

title: Nikkei sinks below 7,000 as the yen soars
what: The Nikkei fell to 6,994.90 on 28 October during the day, its lowest since the bubble. The yen jumped as investors unwound bets financed with cheap yen: the dollar fell from about 106 to about 98 yen during the month. Japan's exporters, from carmakers to electronics firms, face a world recession with a dearer currency.
why: Japan's share of the global crash: exporters such as Sony were hit twice, by collapsing demand and the yen.

title: China announces a 4 trillion yuan stimulus
what: On 9 November China's State Council announced a stimulus of 4 trillion yuan, about $586 billion, with 1.5 trillion for railways, roads and other infrastructure and money for earthquake rebuilding and cheap housing. Growth has fallen towards 6% from double digits.
why: The program pulled China back above 10% growth by mid-2009 and lifted metal prices and the miners, but left the debts that fed the later property bust.

title: China passes Japan as the world's second-largest economy
what: China's economy was larger than Japan's in 2010, which makes China the world's second-largest economy behind the United States. Japan had held that place since before the 1980s. A year ago China also overtook Germany as the world's biggest exporter.
why: The symbolic handover of the arc from Japan to China.

title: Earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima
what: A magnitude 9 earthquake off north-east Japan on 11 March set off a tsunami that left tens of thousands dead or missing, and three reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant were crippled, raising fears of meltdowns. The Nikkei fell more than 10% on 15 March to 8,605. The yen jumped, to about 79 per dollar on 17 March, and the G7 countries sold yen together on 18 March to weaken it.
why: The costliest natural disaster in history, over $300 billion. The yen's strength through 2011 helped bring on Abenomics. Review 2026-10: the meltdowns were confirmed only in May 2011.

title: Abenomics: the yen weakens and Tokyo shares soar
what: Shinzo Abe, whose party won December's election on a promise to end years of falling prices, announced a 10.3 trillion yen stimulus and pressed the Bank of Japan to target 2% inflation. The dollar rose from about 87 yen at the start of January to about 91 at the end. Exporters' shares are leading a rally in Tokyo.
why: Abenomics in action. By May the Tokyo market was up 55%, and exporters such as Sony gained most.

title: Kuroda's 'bazooka': the Bank of Japan doubles the money supply
what: On 4 April the Bank of Japan, under its new governor Haruhiko Kuroda, said it will double the monetary base in two years, buying 60 to 70 trillion yen of bonds a year, to reach 2% inflation. The dollar ended April at about 97 yen.
why: The biggest monetary experiment of its time; it was extended in 2014, joined by negative rates in 2016 and lasted until 2024.

title: China's stock bubble bursts
what: The Shanghai Composite index, which had risen more than 150% in a year on borrowed money, reached a high of about 5,166 on 12 June and lost 30% in three weeks. By 8 and 9 July about 1,400 companies, more than half of all those listed, had halted trading in their shares, and the government stepped in to support prices.
why: The second Chinese mania and its bust; it set up the August devaluation scare. Review 2026-10: 'peaked' was hindsight.

title: China devalues the yuan; 'Black Monday' in Shanghai
what: On 11 August China's central bank cut the yuan by 1.9% and lowered it again on 14 August. On 24 August the Shanghai index fell 8.5%, and the Dow opened 1,000 points lower before closing down 588. Investors fear China's growth is slowing more than Beijing admits.
why: The China scare that gave Wall Street its first sharp fall in years and hit commodity stocks such as Glencore hard.

title: China's circuit breakers trip; Japan goes negative
what: Chinese shares fell about 7% on 4 and 7 January, setting off new circuit breakers that closed the market; on 7 January trading lasted less than 30 minutes. World markets fell with them. At the end of the month the Bank of Japan cut a key rate below zero, to -0.1%.
why: The second China scare. Japan's negative rate showed how little room was left after 25 years of easing.

title: The US-China trade war begins
what: On 6 July the US put tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese imports, and China answered in kind. President Trump started the dispute in March, citing unfair trade practices and theft of intellectual property, and threatens tariffs on far more.
why: The start of a confrontation that outlasted Trump's first term and returned with force in 2025.

title: Trade truce, then Huawei's finance chief is arrested
what: At the G20 summit on 1 December the US and China agreed a 90-day pause in new tariffs. The same day Canada arrested Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer, at the request of the US, which became known a few days later. US tariffs of 10% have applied to $200 billion of Chinese goods since September.
why: Doubts about the truce, together with Fed rate rises, drove Wall Street's worst month in years.

title: Tariffs raised to 25%; Huawei blacklisted
what: Talks broke down and on 10 May the US raised tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods from 10% to 25%. Later in the month Washington restricted Huawei's access to American technology.
why: The trade war's escalation in 2019, which hit chip stocks such as Nvidia hardest.

title: A trade deal, then Wuhan is locked down
what: On 15 January the US and China signed a 'phase one' trade deal: China will buy $200 billion more of US goods and services over two years. On 23 January China sealed off the city of Wuhan to stop a new coronavirus, and lockdowns spread to other cities.
why: The deal was overtaken within days by the pandemic, which started China's three years of zero-Covid.

title: Buffett buys into Japan's trading houses
what: Berkshire Hathaway said it has bought just over 5% of each of Japan's five biggest trading houses, Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, over the past year, worth over $6 billion.
why: The most famous vote of confidence in Japan's revival; Berkshire later raised its stakes to about 10% as Tokyo hit records.

title: China turns on Didi days after its New York listing
what: Didi, China's ride-hailing giant, raised $4.4 billion in New York on 30 June at a value of nearly $70 billion. On 4 July China's internet regulator ordered app stores to remove Didi, citing its handling of personal data. Chinese shares listed abroad are falling. In November 2020 regulators had halted the $34.5 billion share sale of Jack Ma's Ant Group two days before listing.
why: The clearest sign that Beijing put control ahead of markets; Didi left the New York exchange in 2022.

title: Evergrande, owing $300 billion, misses payments
what: China Evergrande, the country's most indebted property developer with about 2 trillion yuan ($310 billion) of liabilities, missed an interest payment of $83.5 million on foreign bonds on 24 September. Beijing's 2020 limits on developers' borrowing have cut off its credit.
why: The start of the property bust: Evergrande was declared in default in December and ordered to liquidate by a Hong Kong court in January 2024, Country Garden followed in 2023, and property, about a quarter of China's economy at its peak, has shrunk ever since.

title: Shanghai locked down
what: Shanghai, China's biggest city with about 25 million people, has been under lockdown since late March as China holds to its zero-Covid policy. Factories and the port are disrupted.
why: The peak of zero-Covid's economic cost; China grew only about 3% in 2022.

title: America cuts China off from advanced chips
what: On 7 October the US banned the export to China of advanced computing chips, of the kind used in AI such as Nvidia's A100 and H100, and of the equipment to make advanced chips.
why: The technology front of the US-China contest, tightened several times since; it shaped Nvidia's China business and spurred China's own AI efforts.

title: The yen falls past 150 per dollar
what: The dollar reached 151 yen on 21 October, the yen's weakest since 1990, as US rates rise while the Bank of Japan keeps its rates below zero. Japan's Finance Ministry has bought yen in September and October, its first such intervention since 1998.
why: The cost of Japan staying alone with ultra-low rates; it forced the first policy change in December.

title: China abandons zero-Covid
what: After protests in late November, set off by a deadly fire in Urumqi, China on 7 December dropped compulsory testing and quarantine in camps, and on 12 December switched off its health-code tracking app. Nearly three years of lockdowns are ending.
why: The reopening was expected to lift China's economy, but the property bust and weak confidence kept growth low.

title: Nikkei beats its 1989 record, 34 years later
what: On 22 February the Nikkei closed at 39,098.68, above its record of 38,915.87 set on 29 December 1989. Foreign investors are buying Japan as companies reform and prices rise again, and as money leaves China.
why: The end of the thirty-year round trip, the closing image of Japan's bust.

title: Tokyo's worst day since 1987 as the yen snaps back
what: The yen hit 161 per dollar in July, its weakest in 37 years, and then the Bank of Japan, which had ended eight years of negative rates in March, raised rates again on 31 July. As traders unwound bets funded with cheap yen, the dollar fell to about 143 yen and on 5 August the Nikkei fell 12.4%, 4,451 points, to 31,458. The next day it gained more than 3,200 points, its biggest daily rise.
why: A two-day panic, not a turn: the Nikkei was back at records within months.

title: China's DeepSeek shakes the AI trade
what: The Chinese start-up DeepSeek released its R1 AI model on 20 January, saying it matches US rivals at a fraction of the cost and on older chips. By 27 January its chatbot was the most downloaded free app in the US, and Nvidia's shares fell about 18%.
why: Showed that US chip controls had not stopped Chinese AI; a sharp but short scare for Nvidia.

title: Tariffs of 145% on China
what: On 2 April President Trump announced tariffs on most of the world, 34% on China. After China retaliated, the US raised its tariff on Chinese goods to 104% and then 145%; China replied with 125%. Trade between the two biggest economies is close to a halt.
why: The trade war's climax; markets fell sharply early in the month and recovered much of the loss by its end.

title: Geneva truce cuts US-China tariffs
what: On 12 May the US and China agreed in Geneva to cut their tariffs for 90 days, the US from 145% to 30% and China from 125% to 10%. Shares rallied around the world.
why: The de-escalation that let the 2025 bull market resume.

title: Takaichi takes over; Nikkei passes 50,000
what: Sanae Takaichi won the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party on 4 October and became Japan's first woman prime minister on 21 October. The Nikkei jumped 4.75% past 47,000 after her win and passed 50,000 on 27 October, on hopes of more government spending.
why: Japan's market at heights unimaginable in the lost decades, with a weak yen as the flip side.

title: Nikkei passes 60,000
what: The Nikkei reached 60,000 for the first time on 23 April, two months after Takaichi's party won a two-thirds majority in the lower house on 8 February, the first party to do so since the war.
why: More than 50% above the 1989 peak in nominal terms.

title: Japan spends a record sum defending the yen
what: The dollar reached about 164 yen on 23 July, and Japan's Finance Ministry said it spent a record 15.4 trillion yen, about $96 billion, buying yen in its interventions, its largest monthly intervention ever. The Nikkei passed 70,000 in June.
why: The other side of Japan's boom: a currency at levels last seen in the 1980s, before the Plaza Accord's effects had run their course.
